examName: Notary Public Exam (General / National Notary Association Style)
tagline: Learn core notary duties and best practices (note: exact requirements vary by state).

domains.name: Notarial Acts and Powers
domains.description: The core notarial acts a commissioned notary is authorized to perform and how they differ.

domains.name: Identifying Signers
domains.description: Establishing the identity of a document signer through satisfactory evidence.

domains.name: Duties and Responsibilities
domains.description: The notary's role as an impartial witness and the proper steps of a notarization.

domains.name: Recordkeeping and the Notary Journal
domains.description: Maintaining an accurate journal of notarial acts and related records.

domains.name: Fraud Prevention and Ethics
domains.description: Deterring fraud and upholding ethical and impartiality standards.

domains.name: Legal Liability
domains.description: The notary's exposure to civil, criminal, and administrative liability for misconduct or negligence.

questions.stem: A signer brings a deed and asks the notary to complete an acknowledgment. What is the signer essentially declaring when they acknowledge a document before a notary?

options.text: That they signed the document willingly and that it is their act and deed
That every statement in the document is true and accurate
That the notary has reviewed the document for legal sufficiency
That the document was signed in the notary's physical presence moments earlier

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In an acknowledgment the signer declares to the notary that they executed the document willingly for the purposes stated; the notary verifies identity and that the act was free and voluntary. Why the others are wrong: **B** that describes a jurat/oath, where the signer swears to the truth of contents; **C** notaries never vouch for a document's legal sufficiency and must not give legal advice; **D** an acknowledgment generally does not require the signer to sign in the notary's presence, only to personally appear and acknowledge the signature.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps of performing a jurat on an affidavit in the correct order, from first to last.

options.text: Require the signer to personally appear before the notary
Confirm the signer's identity through satisfactory evidence
Have the signer sign the affidavit and swear (or affirm) to the truth of its contents before the notary
Complete the jurat certificate ('subscribed and sworn to before me'), then date and affix the seal

questions.explanation: For a jurat the notary first requires the signer to personally appear, then confirms the signer's identity through satisfactory evidence, because every later step depends on knowing who is before the notary. The signer then signs the affidavit and swears or affirms to the truth of its contents in the notary's presence — a jurat requires both signing before the notary and an oath or affirmation. Finally the notary completes the jurat certificate ('subscribed and sworn to before me'), dates it, and affixes the seal to authenticate the act.

questions.stem: While administering an oath, a notary asks the signer to raise their right hand and respond aloud. What is the essential purpose of administering an oath or affirmation?

options.text: To create a religious obligation that all signers must accept
To bind the person's conscience to tell the truth, making a false statement punishable as perjury
To transfer legal responsibility for the document's contents to the notary
To confirm the notary has read the document and agrees with it

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An oath (or its secular equivalent, an affirmation) is a solemn promise that compels truthfulness; a knowingly false statement made under it can constitute perjury. Why the others are wrong: **A** an affirmation is offered precisely so no religious reference is required, so an oath is not mandatory for everyone; **C** the notary never assumes responsibility for content; **D** the notary does not read or endorse the document's substance.

questions.stem: A customer asks a notary to certify that a photocopy of their college diploma is a true and accurate copy of the original. How should the notary generally respond?

options.text: Certify the copy after the customer signs an affidavit swearing it is accurate
Refuse, because notaries are never permitted to certify copies of any document
Make the copy themselves (or compare it to the original) and complete a copy certification only if their state authorizes notaries to certify copies
Direct the customer to record the diploma with the county recorder instead

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Where copy certification is authorized, the notary compares the copy to the original (often making the copy themselves) and certifies it is a true reproduction; this power is state-specific and commonly excludes vital and public records. Why the others are wrong: **B** many states do permit copy certification, so a blanket refusal is inaccurate; **A** a copy certification is the notary's own comparison, not a signer's sworn statement; **D** recording is unrelated and does not address the request.

questions.stem: A document arrives with no notarial certificate wording attached. The signer cannot tell the notary whether an acknowledgment or a jurat is needed. What should the notary do?

options.text: Decline all notarization until the signer hires an attorney
Choose an acknowledgment because it is the most common act
Advise the signer which certificate the document legally needs
Ask the signer (or the document's issuing agency) to specify the type of notarization required, then attach the matching certificate

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The notary may ask the signer what act is required or have them check with the receiving agency, then attach the appropriate certificate; the notary may explain the difference between acts but not pick one for the signer. Why the others are wrong: **B** guessing the act risks an improper notarization; **C** telling the signer which act the document legally requires is unauthorized practice of law; **A** an attorney is unnecessary when the signer can simply confirm the required act.

questions.stem: After completing a notarial certificate, the notary affixes their official seal or stamp. What is the primary purpose of the notary's seal?

options.text: To authenticate the notarial act and identify the notary, often making the document acceptable for recording
To certify that the notary agrees with the contents of the document
To replace the need for a written notarial certificate
To guarantee the document will be accepted in every foreign country

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The seal authenticates the act and identifies the commissioned notary; many recording offices require a legible seal alongside the certificate. Why the others are wrong: **B** the seal never signifies agreement with content; **C** the seal supplements the certificate but does not replace the required certificate wording; **D** foreign acceptance commonly requires additional authentication such as an apostille, which the seal alone does not provide.

questions.stem: A signer presents a document where the preprinted notarial certificate says 'acknowledged before me,' but the signer says they want to swear to the truth of the contents. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Perform the acknowledgment as preprinted, since changing wording is never allowed
Determine the correct act with the signer; if a jurat is needed, attach a jurat certificate and administer an oath
Cross out 'acknowledged' and write in 'sworn' without any other change
Notarize using both certificates simultaneously to be safe

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The wording must match the act actually performed; if the signer needs to swear to contents, the notary administers an oath and attaches a jurat certificate. Why the others are wrong: **A** performing the wrong act to preserve preprinted wording is improper; **C** simply editing one word leaves a certificate that no longer reflects a proper, complete jurat; **D** stacking two contradictory certificates creates an invalid, confusing record.

questions.stem: A signer asks the notary to witness their signature on a document that has no oath language and no acknowledgment wording, just a line for a notary to confirm the signature was made. This describes which notarial act?

options.text: An acknowledgment
A jurat
Signature witnessing
A protest of a negotiable instrument

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** In a signature witnessing, the notary verifies the signer's identity and watches them sign, then certifies the signature was made in the notary's presence, without administering an oath. Why the others are wrong: **B** a jurat requires an oath/affirmation as to the truth of contents; **A** an acknowledgment is the signer declaring a signature is their voluntary act, not the notary watching it being made; **D** a protest concerns dishonored negotiable instruments, an unrelated specialized act.

questions.stem: Which two elements are essential to a complete notarial certificate for a typical acknowledgment? (Select two.)

options.text: The venue (the state and county where the act is performed)
The notary's official signature and seal with commission information
The notary's personal opinion on whether the document is legally valid
The signer's bank account number for verification

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A proper certificate states the venue where the notarization occurred and bears the notary's signature and seal with commission details, which authenticate the act. Why the others are wrong: **C** a notary must never opine on legal validity, as that is unauthorized practice of law; **D** a signer's financial account information is irrelevant and improper to collect for a notarization.

questions.stem: A signer requests a jurat but objects to swearing any oath on religious grounds. How should the notary proceed?

options.text: Have the signer sign a waiver releasing the notary from administering anything
Refuse the notarization because a jurat always requires a religious oath
Perform an acknowledgment instead, since it requires no truthfulness pledge
Offer an affirmation, a solemn secular pledge of truthfulness that carries the same legal effect as an oath

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An affirmation is the secular equivalent of an oath; it carries identical legal weight and is offered to signers who object to swearing, so the jurat can still be completed. Why the others are wrong: **B** refusing is wrong because affirmations exist for exactly this situation; **C** swapping to an acknowledgment changes the act the document requires; **A** a waiver cannot substitute for the truthfulness pledge a jurat demands.

questions.stem: Before notarizing, a notary must be satisfied of the signer's identity. Which method provides the strongest, most direct basis for identifying a signer?

options.text: Personal knowledge of the signer built up over time so the notary is certain of who they are
The signer's verbal statement of their own name
A business card the signer hands to the notary
Recognition of the signer's voice over the telephone

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Personal knowledge means the notary knows the individual well enough through prior dealings to be certain of their identity, the most direct form of identification. Why the others are wrong: **B** a signer simply stating their name proves nothing; **C** a business card is trivially fabricated and is not acceptable identification; **D** a voice on the phone does not establish identity for an in-person act and is not a recognized ID method.

questions.stem: A signer the notary has never met presents identification. Which document is generally the most appropriate form of identification to rely on?

options.text: A recent utility bill addressed to the signer
A current government-issued photo ID showing the signer's photograph, signature, and physical description
A Social Security card
A library membership card with the signer's name

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A current government-issued ID bearing a photograph, signature, and description (such as a driver's license or passport) is the standard acceptable identification in most states. Why the others are wrong: **A** a utility bill has no photo and is easily forged; **C** a Social Security card carries no photo and is not an identity document; **D** a library card is not government-issued and lacks a photo, so it cannot establish identity.

questions.stem: A signer has no acceptable ID and the notary does not personally know them. The signer offers to bring people who can vouch for their identity. What is the correct term and general role for these people?

options.text: Co-signers, who sign the document alongside the signer
Character references, who describe the signer's reputation in the community
Credible identifying witnesses, who personally know the signer and swear to the signer's identity under oath
Subscribing witnesses, who notarize the document on the signer's behalf

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** When ID and personal knowledge are unavailable, many states allow one or two credible identifying witnesses who personally know the signer to swear under oath to the signer's identity. Why the others are wrong: **B** vouching for reputation is not the same as swearing to identity; **A** co-signers are parties to the document, not identity proof; **D** a subscribing witness is unrelated and cannot notarize, since only a commissioned notary performs the act.

questions.stem: During a notarization, the signer appears confused, cannot explain what the document is, and keeps asking where they are. What should the notary do?

options.text: Have the signer drink water and continue after a short break
Proceed, since assessing awareness is not part of the notary's duty
Notarize only if a family member signs on the confused signer's behalf
Decline to notarize, because the signer must appear aware and able to understand the act

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A notary must reasonably assess that the signer is aware of what they are signing; if the signer appears unable to comprehend the act, the notary should decline. Why the others are wrong: **B** assessing apparent awareness and willingness is a core notarial duty; **C** a family member cannot substitute their understanding for the signer's, and signing for another raises serious authority issues; **A** a break does not resolve a genuine lack of comprehension.

questions.stem: A signer at a bank says her employer told her she 'has' to sign the loan papers today even though she does not want to. The notary observes she is being pressured. What should the notary do?

options.text: Decline the notarization, because the signer must act willingly and free of coercion
Proceed, because willingness is the employer's concern, not the notary's
Notarize but write 'signed under protest' on the certificate
Ask the employer to confirm the signer consents and then proceed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A notarization requires the signer to act of their own free will; visible coercion is grounds to refuse. Why the others are wrong: **B** confirming willingness is squarely the notary's responsibility; **C** altering the certificate does not cure a lack of genuine consent and is improper; **D** relying on the very person applying the pressure does not establish the signer's free will.

questions.stem: A signer is physically unable to sign their name due to an injury but is fully alert and willing. In most states, how may the notarization proceed?

options.text: The notary signs the document for the signer and notarizes their own signature
The signer may direct another person to sign their name for them, in the signer's presence and at their direction, following the state's signature-by-mark or directed-signature rules
The notarization is impossible and must be refused outright
A relative signs at home and brings the document back for notarization

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Most states permit a signature by mark or a directed signature, where a disinterested person signs the signer's name at the signer's direction and in their presence, often with witnesses. Why the others are wrong: **A** a notary cannot sign for the signer and then notarize, which is a conflict and improper; **C** disability does not bar notarization when proper procedures exist; **D** signing outside the notary's presence defeats the requirement of personal appearance.

questions.stem: When examining a government-issued photo ID for identifying a signer, which two checks should a notary make? (Select two.)

options.text: Confirm the ID is current/unexpired (or within any state-allowed grace period)
Compare the photograph and physical description to the person appearing
Verify the signer's credit score from the ID number
Confirm the ID lists the signer's place of employment

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The notary should confirm the ID is current and compare its photo and description against the person present to be satisfied of identity. Why the others are wrong: **C** credit scores are irrelevant to identity and cannot be derived from an ID; **D** employment information is neither expected on an ID nor relevant to verifying who the signer is.

questions.stem: A notary's longtime neighbor, whom the notary knows well, needs a document notarized but forgot their wallet. How may the notary verify identity?

options.text: Accept the neighbor's spoken assurance of who they are without more
Refuse, because photo ID is the only acceptable method in every case
Rely on personal knowledge of the neighbor's identity
Ask the neighbor to text a photo of their ID from home

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Personal knowledge is an accepted basis for identification; if the notary genuinely knows the neighbor, an ID is not required. Why the others are wrong: **B** photo ID is one method but not the only one, since personal knowledge and credible witnesses also exist; **A** a stranger's spoken assurance would be insufficient, but here actual personal knowledge is the operative basis; **D** a texted photo of an ID is not the signer presenting a verifiable original and is not an accepted method.

questions.stem: A signer presents a credible identifying witness whom the notary does not personally know and who has no ID either. In most states, what is the problem with relying on this witness?

options.text: A single credible witness is always sufficient regardless of the notary knowing them
Credible witnesses are never permitted under any circumstances
A credible witness must be a licensed attorney
A credible witness must themselves be known to the notary or be identified by acceptable ID, and must personally know the signer

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A credible witness must be reliable to the notary, either personally known to the notary or proven by acceptable ID, and must personally know the signer; an unknown, unidentified witness fails this test. Why the others are wrong: **B** credible witnesses are commonly allowed; **C** there is no attorney requirement; **A** sufficiency rules vary, but an unverifiable witness can never be relied upon.

questions.stem: How is the fundamental role of a notary public best described?

options.text: An impartial, third-party witness to the signing of documents who verifies identity and deters fraud
A legal advisor who ensures documents serve the signer's best interests
An advocate who represents the interests of whichever party is paying the fee
A government official who decides whether a document is legally enforceable

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A notary is a neutral, impartial witness who confirms the identity and willingness of signers and helps deter fraud, without taking sides. Why the others are wrong: **B** notaries are barred from giving legal advice unless also licensed attorneys; **C** impartiality forbids advocating for any party; **D** notaries do not adjudicate enforceability or the legal effect of documents.

questions.stem: A signer mails a notary a document already signed and asks the notary to notarize it and mail it back, since they trust each other. What is the controlling problem with this request?

options.text: The notary may proceed because the signer's trust substitutes for appearance
The signer must personally appear before the notary at the time of notarization
The notary may proceed only if the signer's signature looks genuine
The notary may proceed if the signer confirms by phone that they signed it

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Personal appearance is a cornerstone of notarization; the signer must be physically present (or present via authorized remote technology) before the notary, who cannot notarize a signature made in their absence. Why the others are wrong: **A** trust never replaces appearance; **C** judging whether a signature 'looks genuine' is not a substitute for the signer appearing; **D** a phone confirmation does not satisfy the appearance requirement for a traditional notarization.

questions.stem: Arrange the standard steps of performing a typical notarization in the correct order, from first to last.

options.text: Require the signer to personally appear
Verify the signer's identity
Complete the notarial certificate and affix the seal
Record the act in the notary journal

questions.explanation: The notary first requires the signer to personally appear, because every later step depends on the signer being present. Next the notary verifies the signer's identity through personal knowledge, ID, or credible witnesses, and confirms willingness and awareness. The notary then performs the act (administering an oath if a jurat) and completes the notarial certificate and seal to authenticate it. Finally the notary records the act in the journal, capturing the details for the permanent record. This earliest-to-latest sequence reflects standard practice: appearance and identity must be settled before the certificate is signed, and the journal entry documents what was just done.

questions.stem: A signer presents a document with several blank spaces left unfilled and asks the notary to notarize it anyway. What should the notary do?

options.text: Notarize it and note 'incomplete' on the certificate
Fill in the blanks for the signer and then notarize
Decline to notarize an incomplete document, as blanks invite later fraudulent alteration
Notarize because completeness of the document is never the notary's concern

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A notary should not notarize a document containing blank spaces, because material could be added afterward to commit fraud; the signer should complete it first. Why the others are wrong: **B** filling in the document for the signer is improper and risks unauthorized practice of law; **A** a notation does not prevent later alteration of the blanks; **D** while a notary doesn't judge content, obvious blanks are a recognized fraud risk the notary must address.

questions.stem: A notary commissioned in one state is asked to notarize a document while traveling in a neighboring state where they hold no commission. What should the notary do?

options.text: Proceed as long as the signer is a resident of the notary's home state
Proceed, because a notary commission is valid nationwide
Proceed if the document will ultimately be recorded in the notary's home state
Decline, because a notary may only perform notarizations within the jurisdiction of their commission

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A notary's authority is limited to the state (and within it, the geographic area) that commissioned them; acting outside that jurisdiction is improper. Why the others are wrong: **B** commissions are state-specific, not nationwide; **C** the eventual recording location does not extend the notary's territorial authority; **A** the signer's residency does not expand where the notary may lawfully act.

questions.stem: How should a notary store the official seal/stamp and journal when not in use?

options.text: In a locked, secure area accessible only to the notary
In a shared office drawer so coworkers can notarize when the notary is out
With a trusted assistant who can stamp documents on the notary's behalf
At the front desk so customers can self-serve after hours

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The seal and journal must be kept under the notary's exclusive, secured control to prevent misuse and protect the integrity of notarial acts. Why the others are wrong: **B** sharing access lets others perform acts the notary did not, which is prohibited; **C** no one but the commissioned notary may use the seal; **D** leaving notarial tools for self-service is a serious breach enabling fraud.

questions.stem: Which two situations require a notary to refuse to perform a notarization? (Select two.)

options.text: The signer cannot be identified and offers no acceptable proof of identity
The signer appears coerced and unwilling to sign
The document is written in formal legal language the notary finds complex
The signer asks the notary to also serve as a witness signature line elsewhere

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A notary must refuse when identity cannot be established and when the signer is not acting willingly, since both are essential prerequisites. Why the others are wrong: **C** complex legal wording is not a reason to refuse, as the notary does not judge content; **D** signing as a witness elsewhere is a separate question and not, by itself, grounds to refuse the notarization.

questions.stem: A notary's commission has a fixed term that has now expired, but the notary's seal is still in good condition. The notary is asked to perform one quick notarization. What should they do?

options.text: Proceed, because a usable seal means the commission is still valid
Decline, because authority to notarize ends when the commission term expires
Proceed once and then renew the commission afterward
Proceed if the signer agrees not to object to the expired commission

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A notary's power flows from a valid commission for a set term; once it expires, the notary has no authority and must not notarize until recommissioned. Why the others are wrong: **A** the condition of the seal is irrelevant to whether the commission is active; **C** notarizing first and renewing later is acting without authority; **D** a signer cannot consent to give an uncommissioned person notarial power.

questions.stem: Why is keeping a notary journal considered an essential best practice (and a requirement in many states)?

options.text: It substitutes for the notarial certificate on the document
It allows the notary to bill signers a higher fee for record storage
It creates a permanent, chronological record of acts that protects the notary and helps detect or prove fraud
It records the notary's legal opinions about each document

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The journal is a sequential record of every notarization that protects the notary if an act is later questioned and aids fraud investigations. Why the others are wrong: **B** the journal is not a billing device; **A** it supplements but never replaces the certificate placed on the document; **D** a notary records facts of the act, never legal opinions, which they are barred from giving.

questions.stem: Which detail is LEAST appropriate to record in a standard notary journal entry?

options.text: The signer's name and signature
The date and time of the notarization
The type of notarial act performed and the type of identification relied upon
The notary's personal assessment of whether the document is a good legal idea

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The journal records objective facts of the act, not the notary's opinion about the document's wisdom or legality, which the notary is not permitted to judge. Why the others are wrong: **B** the date and time are standard entry contents; **C** the act type and identification method are core required details; **A** the signer's name and signature are routinely recorded in the journal.

questions.stem: In states that require or allow a thumbprint in the journal for sensitive documents like deeds, which two statements about the thumbprint are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: It provides a unique biometric record that can help identify the true signer if the act is later challenged
It is especially valuable for high-fraud-risk documents such as deeds and powers of attorney
It replaces the need to verify the signer's identity beforehand
It guarantees the document can never be contested in court

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A thumbprint is a unique biometric that ties a specific person to the act, and it is most valuable for high-fraud-risk instruments like deeds and powers of attorney where proving the true signer matters. Why the others are wrong: **C** a thumbprint supplements, never replaces, proper up-front identity verification; **D** no record makes a document immune from legal challenge.

questions.stem: A notary leaves their employer to take a new job. The journal contains records of notarizations the notary performed at the old workplace. Who should retain the journal?

options.text: The notary, because the journal is the notary's personal property and responsibility, not the employer's
The employer, because the notarizations occurred on company time
Whichever party paid for the journal book
It should be destroyed upon leaving the job

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The journal belongs to the notary personally and travels with them; an employer generally has no right to keep it, even if notarizations were done at work. Why the others are wrong: **B** performing acts on company time does not transfer ownership to the employer; **C** who purchased the book does not determine custody of the official record; **D** journals must be retained for the required period, not destroyed when changing jobs.

questions.stem: A member of the public asks to flip through the notary's entire journal to browse all past notarizations out of curiosity. How should the notary respond?

options.text: Hand over the journal so anyone may review every entry at will
Decline open browsing; provide only a specific authorized record on proper request, protecting other signers' information
Refuse all access to the journal, even to a court that subpoenas a record
Photocopy the whole journal and post it publicly for transparency

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The journal contains sensitive information about many signers; a notary should furnish only the specific entry that a proper, lawful request identifies, not allow indiscriminate browsing. Why the others are wrong: **A** letting anyone read every entry exposes unrelated signers' data; **C** a notary must comply with a valid subpoena or court order, so blanket refusal is wrong; **D** publishing the journal grossly violates signers' privacy.

questions.stem: A notary receives a valid subpoena directing them to produce a particular journal entry for a court case. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Destroy the entry to avoid getting involved in litigation
Ignore it, because journal entries are always confidential
Comply by producing the specific record the subpoena lawfully requires
Produce the entry only if the signer gives permission first

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A subpoena or court order is a lawful demand, and a notary must produce the specific journal record it requires. Why the others are wrong: **B** confidentiality yields to a valid legal order; **A** destroying a subpoenaed record is obstruction and a serious offense; **D** while signer privacy matters, a valid subpoena does not depend on the signer's consent.

questions.stem: Which two items are commonly part of a complete notary journal entry? (Select two.)

options.text: The type of notarial act performed (e.g., acknowledgment or jurat)
The method used to identify the signer
The notary's prediction of how a court will rule on the document
The home address of every witness the notary has ever used

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A complete entry typically records the type of act performed and how the signer's identity was established. Why the others are wrong: **C** a notary cannot opine on legal outcomes and would never record such a prediction; **D** logging unrelated witnesses' home addresses is neither standard nor appropriate for the entry.

questions.stem: A signer asks a notary, 'Which type of deed should I use to transfer my house to my son?' The notary is not an attorney. How should the notary respond?

options.text: Complete a deed for the signer to keep the process simple
Recommend the deed the notary personally thinks is best
Tell the signer that any deed works the same way legally
Explain they cannot give legal advice and suggest the signer consult an attorney

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Advising which legal document or deed type to use is the practice of law; a non-attorney notary must decline and refer the signer to a qualified attorney. Why the others are wrong: **B** recommending a specific deed is giving legal advice; **C** stating deeds are legally interchangeable is both false and unauthorized legal advice; **A** preparing legal documents for others is unauthorized practice of law.

questions.stem: A notary is asked to notarize a contract in which the notary is personally named as a party who will receive money. What is the ethical problem?

options.text: The notary has a disqualifying financial interest and should not notarize, to preserve impartiality
There is no problem as long as the notary verifies identity
There is no problem because the notary is not the signer
The notary may notarize if they reduce their fee to zero

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A notary must be impartial; having a direct financial or beneficial interest in the transaction is disqualifying, so the notary should not perform the act. Why the others are wrong: **B** verifying identity does not cure a conflict of interest; **C** being a beneficiary, not merely a signer, is exactly what creates the disqualifying interest; **D** waiving the fee does not eliminate the underlying personal stake.

questions.stem: Which two circumstances should a notary treat as warning signs of possible identity or document fraud? (Select two.)

options.text: The name on the document differs significantly from the name on the signer's ID with no plausible explanation
The signer's photo ID appears altered, with a mismatched photo or tampered lamination
The document is several pages long and uses formal legal terms
The signer asks the notary to explain the difference between a jurat and an acknowledgment

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** An unexplained name mismatch between the document and the ID, and an ID that looks altered or tampered with, are classic fraud red flags that should make a notary pause and decline if not satisfied of identity. Why the others are wrong: **C** length and legal terminology are normal and not a fraud signal, and the notary does not judge content; **D** asking the notary to explain the two acts is a proper, routine question, not a warning sign.

questions.stem: A non-attorney notary who is fluent in Spanish advertises their services in Spanish using the title 'notario público.' Why is this commonly considered a deceptive or prohibited practice?

options.text: Advertising notary services in any language other than English is illegal
In many Latin American countries a 'notario público' is a highly trained attorney, so the term can mislead immigrant clients into thinking the notary can give legal advice
Notaries are forbidden from advertising their services at all
The term is fine because it is simply the Spanish translation of 'notary public'

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Because a 'notario público' abroad is an attorney-level official, using the term can deceive immigrants into believing a U.S. notary can provide legal services; many states prohibit or restrict it. Why the others are wrong: **A** advertising in other languages is permitted; **C** notaries may advertise truthfully; **D** despite being a literal translation, the term carries a misleading professional connotation that the law guards against.

questions.stem: Regarding the fees a notary may charge for performing a notarization, which statement reflects the general best practice?

options.text: A notary must always perform notarizations for free
A notary may charge whatever the market will bear with no limit
A notary should charge no more than the maximum fee allowed by their state and avoid undisclosed or excessive charges
A notary may charge more if the document appears legally important

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Most states cap the fee a notary may charge per act; the ethical practice is to stay within that limit and be transparent. Why the others are wrong: **B** charging unlimited fees ignores statutory maximums; **A** notaries are generally permitted to charge a fee, so free service is not required; **D** basing the fee on the document's perceived importance is improper and exceeds allowed charges.

questions.stem: A friend asks a notary to 'just stamp' a document and predate the notarization to last week so it appears timely. What should the notary do?

options.text: Backdate the act but record the true date in the journal
Agree, since it is only a small favor for a friend
Backdate by only a day or two as a compromise
Refuse, because backdating a notarial act is fraudulent and prohibited

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A notary must record the actual date of the act; falsifying or backdating the date is a fraudulent, prohibited act that can lead to criminal and civil liability. Why the others are wrong: **B** doing it as a favor does not make falsification lawful; **C** backdating any amount is still falsification; **A** an accurate journal entry does not legitimize a falsely dated certificate on the document.

questions.stem: Which two practices help a notary deter document and identity fraud? (Select two.)

options.text: Requiring the signer to personally appear and verifying identity carefully
Refusing to notarize documents with blank spaces
Notarizing signatures sent by mail to save the signer a trip
Letting the signer fill in details after the seal is applied

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Insisting on personal appearance with careful identity checks, and refusing documents with blanks that could be altered later, are core fraud-deterrence practices. Why the others are wrong: **C** notarizing a mailed signature violates the appearance requirement and invites fraud; **D** allowing entries after sealing lets the document be changed beyond what was notarized.

questions.stem: A notary carelessly notarizes a forged signature without checking ID, and a homeowner loses property as a result. What type of liability does the notary most directly face?

options.text: Civil liability for negligence, exposing the notary to damages for the harm caused
No liability, because the forger alone is responsible
Liability only if the notary intended to help the fraud
Liability limited strictly to returning the notarization fee

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A notary who fails to exercise reasonable care, such as skipping identity verification, can be civilly liable in negligence for the resulting damages. Why the others are wrong: **B** the notary's own carelessness creates independent liability alongside the forger's; **C** civil negligence does not require intent, only a failure of due care; **D** damages can far exceed the small fee charged.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a notary surety bond that many states require?

options.text: To insure the notary against any personal loss like a malpractice policy
To protect the public by compensating those harmed by the notary's misconduct, with the notary obligated to repay the surety
To pay the notary's salary during the commission term
To guarantee the notary cannot be sued by any signer

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A surety bond protects members of the public who are financially harmed by a notary's improper acts; the surety pays the claimant and the notary must reimburse the surety. Why the others are wrong: **A** the bond protects the public, not the notary; errors-and-omissions insurance protects the notary; **C** a bond is not compensation or salary; **D** a bond does not shield the notary from being sued.

questions.stem: An employer pressures their notary-employee to notarize a document without the signer present, promising to 'take all responsibility.' If the notary complies, who can be held personally responsible?

options.text: Neither party, because the employer accepted responsibility
Only the employer, because they directed the act
The notary remains personally responsible for their own notarial misconduct, regardless of the employer's promise
Only the signer whose signature was notarized

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A notary is personally accountable for their own acts; an employer's promise to assume blame cannot relieve the notary of personal liability for an improper notarization. Why the others are wrong: **B** the notary's personal responsibility does not vanish because an employer directed the act, though the employer may also share liability; **A** a private promise cannot erase legal accountability; **D** the absent signer is not the party who committed the notarial misconduct.

questions.stem: A commissioning authority discovers a notary repeatedly violated notary law. Beyond any court case, what administrative consequence can the authority directly impose?

options.text: Automatic disbarment from practicing law
A criminal prison sentence imposed by the agency itself
A civil damages award paid to private victims
Suspension or revocation of the notary's commission

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The commissioning authority's administrative power includes suspending or revoking the notary's commission for misconduct. Why the others are wrong: **B** prison sentences are criminal penalties imposed by courts, not by the commissioning agency; **C** civil damages are awarded through lawsuits, not administrative action; **A** disbarment applies to attorneys and is irrelevant to a notary commission.

questions.stem: A signer asks what an acknowledgment and a jurat have in common. Which requirement applies to BOTH acts?

options.text: The signer must take an oath swearing the contents are true
The signer must sign the document in the notary's presence
The signer must personally appear before the notary and be identified
The notary must read the document and confirm it is accurate

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Both acts require the signer to personally appear and to be satisfactorily identified by the notary; that is common ground regardless of the act. Why the others are wrong: **A** the oath as to truth of contents is unique to the jurat, not the acknowledgment; **B** signing in the notary's presence is required for a jurat but not for a typical acknowledgment; **D** a notary never reads the document for accuracy or vouches for its contents.

questions.stem: A notary completes an acknowledgment certificate, but the certificate has a blank line for the date of the act. The notary is unsure what date to enter. Which date belongs on the certificate?

options.text: The date the signer originally signed the document at home
The date the notarial act is actually performed before the notary
The date the document will be recorded or filed
The date the document was drafted by its preparer

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The certificate must show the date the notarial act takes place in the notary's presence, because that is the act being certified. Why the others are wrong: **A** an earlier signing date is irrelevant to when the notarization occurred, and using it would misstate the act; **C** a future recording date does not reflect when the notary acted; **D** the drafting date concerns the document's creation, not the notarization.

questions.stem: A signer presents a multi-page contract for notarization. The preprinted acknowledgment certificate is on a separate page that does not name the document or its date. What is the recommended best practice?

options.text: Staple the certificate to any nearby document so it is not lost
Add identifying details to the loose certificate (such as document title, date, and number of pages) so it cannot be detached and reused on another document
Refuse, because a notary may never use a certificate printed on a separate page
Leave the certificate blank except for the seal to keep it flexible

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A loose or attached certificate should reference the document it belongs to (title, date, page count) so it cannot be removed and fraudulently reattached elsewhere. Why the others are wrong: **C** separate-page (loose) certificates are commonly permitted when properly secured and described; **A** stapling alone, with no identifying details, still leaves the certificate vulnerable to misuse; **D** leaving the certificate blank invites exactly the fraud the identifying details are meant to prevent.

questions.stem: A signer brings a sworn statement and asks the notary to perform a 'verification on oath or affirmation.' Which description best matches this act?

options.text: The notary certifies that a photocopy is a true copy of an original
The signer declares a previously made signature is their voluntary act, without swearing to contents
The signer appears, swears or affirms the statement is true, and signs it before the notary, who then certifies the oath and signing
The notary witnesses a signature being made but administers no oath

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A verification on oath or affirmation is the modern name for a jurat: the signer appears, swears or affirms the contents are true, signs before the notary, and the notary certifies it. Why the others are wrong: **B** that describes an acknowledgment, which involves no oath; **D** that describes a signature witnessing, which also has no oath; **A** that describes a copy certification, an unrelated act.

questions.stem: A notary's official stamp partially overlaps the signature line and smudges, leaving the seal hard to read on a deed bound for the county recorder. What is the best response?

options.text: Leave the smudged seal, since one impression is legally sufficient no matter its clarity
Affix a fresh, legible seal impression in a clear area of the same page so the recording office can read it
Sign their name in place of the seal and omit the stamp entirely
Photocopy the page so the seal looks darker

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The seal must be legible, especially for recording; the notary should add a clear, complete impression in an open area so the document is acceptable. Why the others are wrong: **A** an illegible seal can cause the recorder to reject the document, so clarity does matter; **C** the seal generally cannot be replaced by just a signature when a stamp is required; **D** photocopying the page does not create a valid original notarial seal.

questions.stem: Which two acts require the notary to administer an oath or affirmation? (Select two.)

options.text: Taking a jurat (verification on oath or affirmation) on an affidavit
Swearing in a credible identifying witness who vouches for a signer's identity
Performing a standard acknowledgment on a deed
Certifying that a copy is a true reproduction of an original

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A jurat requires the notary to administer an oath/affirmation as to the truth of the contents, and a credible witness must be placed under oath to swear to the signer's identity. Why the others are wrong: **C** an acknowledgment involves no oath, only the signer's declaration of voluntary signing; **D** a copy certification is the notary's own comparison and involves no oath.

questions.stem: A signer asks a notary to certify a copy of a certified birth certificate they received from a vital records office. In most states, how should the notary handle this?

options.text: Certify the copy, since notaries may certify any document on request
Decline to certify the copy, because vital and publicly recordable records are commonly excluded; the signer should obtain a certified copy from the issuing agency
Certify it only after the signer swears the copy is accurate
Certify it and add a note that the original is on file with the state

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Copy certification, where authorized, commonly excludes vital records (birth, death, marriage) and other publicly recordable documents; those copies come from the issuing agency. Why the others are wrong: **A** notaries cannot certify just any document, and many are expressly excluded; **C** a signer's sworn statement is not a notary copy certification; **D** a note does not cure the prohibition on certifying a vital record.

questions.stem: A notarial certificate includes the line 'State of ___, County of ___' at the top. What does this venue information indicate?

options.text: The state and county where the notarial act is performed
The state and county where the signer permanently resides
The state and county where the document will be used or recorded
The birthplace of the signer named in the document

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The venue states the location (state and county) where the notarization actually takes place, anchoring the act to the notary's jurisdiction. Why the others are wrong: **B** the signer's residence is not what the venue records; **C** the eventual place of use or recording is unrelated to the venue of the act; **D** the signer's birthplace has nothing to do with the venue line.

questions.stem: A signer wants the notary to administer a verbal oath to a witness who will testify at a private hearing, with no document to sign. May a notary administer a standalone oath like this?

options.text: No, a notary may only administer an oath attached to a written, signed document
Yes, administering oaths and affirmations is a recognized notarial power that can stand alone, where state law permits
No, only judges may administer any oath
Yes, but only if the notary also gives the witness legal advice about testifying

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Administering oaths and affirmations is itself a notarial act and can be performed on its own (for example, before testimony) where the state authorizes it. Why the others are wrong: **A** an oath need not always be tied to a signed document; **C** notaries, not only judges, are commonly empowered to administer oaths; **D** a notary must never give legal advice, so that condition is improper.

questions.stem: A signer's name on a deed reads 'Margaret A. Collins,' but her current photo ID reads 'Maggie Collins.' She explains 'Maggie' is just her nickname. How should a notary generally handle the name discrepancy?

options.text: Proceed only if the notary is satisfied the ID reasonably establishes the signer is the person named on the document; a clearly informal nickname alone may not match the legal name
Proceed automatically, because any ID with the same last name is always sufficient
Change the name on the deed to match the ID
Refuse forever, since a name can never differ between an ID and a document

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The notary must be satisfied the ID proves the signer is the person named on the document; a name that does not reasonably match may require better ID rather than guessing. Why the others are wrong: **B** a shared last name alone does not guarantee identity; **C** altering the document's name is improper and outside the notary's role; **D** names can legitimately vary, so a permanent refusal misstates the rule.

questions.stem: A signer presents a foreign passport with a photograph as identification. Generally, why is a passport widely accepted as satisfactory identification?

options.text: Because it lists the signer's home address for verification
Because it is a government-issued document bearing the bearer's photograph and signature
Because it proves the signer is a U.S. citizen
Because it cannot be forged under any circumstances

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A passport is government-issued and carries a photo and signature, the core features that make an ID satisfactory for identifying a signer in most states. Why the others are wrong: **A** passports typically do not list a home address, and address is not what makes an ID acceptable; **C** a passport shows the issuing country, not necessarily U.S. citizenship, which is irrelevant to identity for notarization; **D** no document is impossible to forge, which is why the notary still inspects it.

questions.stem: In a state that allows TWO credible identifying witnesses when a signer has no ID, what is the typical rule about whether the notary must personally know those witnesses?

options.text: Both witnesses must always be the notary's close relatives
When two credible witnesses are used, they commonly need not be personally known to the notary but must themselves present acceptable ID and personally know the signer
The witnesses never need any identification of their own
Two witnesses are never permitted; only one is ever allowed

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Where two credible witnesses are allowed, they commonly need not be known to the notary but must prove their own identity with acceptable ID and must personally know the signer. Why the others are wrong: **A** there is no requirement that witnesses be the notary's relatives, indeed that could create a conflict; **C** witnesses unknown to the notary must show their own ID; **D** two witnesses are expressly permitted in many states.

questions.stem: Which two requirements must a credible identifying witness satisfy to be relied upon? (Select two.)

options.text: The witness must personally know the signer whose identity they vouch for
The witness must have a direct financial interest in the document
The witness must take an oath or affirmation as to the signer's identity
The witness must be a co-owner of the property described in the document

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** A credible witness must personally know the signer and must swear or affirm under oath to the signer's identity. Why the others are wrong: **B** a financial interest in the document would disqualify the witness as biased, not qualify them; **D** being a co-owner makes the witness an interested party, which undermines the impartial purpose of the witness.

questions.stem: A signer is blind and cannot read the document. The signer is alert, willing, and properly identified. What is the appropriate way for the notary to proceed?

options.text: Refuse, because a blind person can never be notarized
Proceed; the notary may have the document read to the signer (often by a disinterested person) so the signer understands what is being signed, then complete the act
Sign the document for the signer since they cannot see it
Skip identity verification because reading the document is enough

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A blind signer can be accommodated, commonly by having the document read aloud (ideally by a disinterested party) so the signer is aware of its nature before signing. Why the others are wrong: **A** a disability is not grounds to refuse when the signer is aware and willing; **C** the notary cannot sign for the signer; **D** identity must still be verified regardless of whether the document is read aloud.

questions.stem: A signer who does not speak the notary's language brings a friend to translate the entire transaction. Why is relying on a third-party interpreter generally discouraged for a notarization?

options.text: Because translation is illegal in all notarizations
Because the notary must communicate directly with the signer to confirm willingness and awareness, and an interpreter can introduce error or undue influence
Because the interpreter automatically becomes the legal signer
Because using an interpreter doubles the maximum fee the notary may charge

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A notary should communicate directly with the signer to gauge willingness and awareness; a go-between can distort the exchange or exert influence, so direct communication is the best practice. Why the others are wrong: **A** translation is not categorically illegal; **C** an interpreter does not become the signer; **D** fees relate to the act performed, not to whether an interpreter is present.

questions.stem: A signer presents a driver's license that expired three months ago. The state allows IDs within a limited grace period after expiration. The notary cannot recall the exact rule. What is the most prudent course?

options.text: Always accept any expired ID, since the photo still shows the person
Always reject any expired ID without exception
Verify the state's specific rule on expired IDs before relying on it, and if unsure or the ID falls outside any allowed window, ask for current acceptable identification
Accept it only if the signer promises to renew the license soon

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Rules on expired IDs vary, so the prudent notary confirms the state's specific allowance and, if the ID is outside any window or the rule is unclear, requests current acceptable ID. Why the others are wrong: **A** blanket acceptance ignores requirements that an ID be current or within a defined grace period; **B** a flat rejection is wrong where the state explicitly permits a grace period; **D** a promise to renew does not make an expired ID acceptable.

questions.stem: Why does a notary visually compare the photograph on an ID to the person standing in front of them, rather than just reading the name?

options.text: To confirm the person presenting the ID is actually its rightful holder and matches the document
To judge whether the signer looks trustworthy enough to sign
To estimate the signer's age for the document
To decide whether the document is legally valid

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Comparing the photo and description to the person present helps ensure the ID belongs to that individual and that they are the signer named, the core of identity verification. Why the others are wrong: **B** a notary does not assess a signer's character or trustworthiness; **C** estimating age is not the purpose of the photo comparison; **D** judging legal validity is outside the notary's role and is unauthorized practice of law.

questions.stem: A real estate agent offers a notary a bonus for every loan signing the notary 'helps close' by encouraging hesitant borrowers to sign. Why should the notary decline this arrangement?

options.text: Because encouraging signers to sign and being paid to influence the outcome compromises the notary's required impartiality
Because notaries may never be paid for any notarization
Because only attorneys may notarize loan documents
Because the notary would have to give the borrowers legal advice

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A notary must remain a neutral witness; being paid to push hesitant signers toward signing destroys impartiality and pressures the signer's free will. Why the others are wrong: **B** notaries may charge proper fees for the act itself, so payment per se is not the problem; **C** notaries, not just attorneys, may notarize loan documents; **D** the arrangement's flaw is the loss of neutrality, not a requirement to give legal advice (which is itself prohibited).

questions.stem: A notary realizes that, by law and custom, they may refuse a notarization for a proper reason without being liable. Which reason is a legitimate basis to refuse?

options.text: The signer belongs to a religion the notary dislikes
The signer cannot be satisfactorily identified
The signer is of a certain national origin
The notary simply prefers not to serve walk-in customers of a certain race

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Inability to establish the signer's identity is a proper, lawful ground to refuse, since identification is a prerequisite to any notarization. Why the others are wrong: **A** refusing based on religion is unlawful discrimination, not a valid reason; **C** national origin is a protected characteristic and not a legitimate basis; **D** refusing service based on race is illegal discrimination, never a proper ground.

questions.stem: A notary moves to a new home address and changes their legal last name after marriage. Regarding their commission, what is the general best practice?

options.text: Ignore the changes, because a commission is unaffected by personal information updates
Notify the commissioning authority of the changes as required, and follow the state's procedure before signing under a new name
Immediately stop notarizing permanently
Continue signing the old name indefinitely to avoid paperwork

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Notaries are generally required to report changes such as address or legal name to the commissioning authority and to follow the state's process (which may involve an updated seal) before notarizing under the new name. Why the others are wrong: **A** these changes typically must be reported; **D** signing a name that no longer matches the commission record is improper; **C** a name or address change does not end the commission, so stopping permanently is unnecessary.

questions.stem: After a signer leaves, a notary notices they wrote the wrong county in the venue and made a typo in the signer's name on the certificate. What is the appropriate way to handle the error?

options.text: Use correction fluid to white out and overwrite the certificate
Quietly discard the document and pretend the act never happened
Correct it properly per state practice (typically by lining through the error, entering the correct information, and initialing/dating), or complete a new, accurate certificate
Leave the errors, since a notarial certificate can never be corrected

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Errors should be corrected transparently, commonly by lining through the mistake, adding the correct information, and initialing, or by attaching a fresh, accurate certificate. Why the others are wrong: **A** correction fluid hides changes and looks like tampering; **B** discarding a completed act and concealing it is improper; **D** certificates can be corrected through accepted methods, so leaving known errors is wrong.

questions.stem: A signer requests an acknowledgment on a power of attorney. Arrange the notary's steps in the correct order, from first to last.

options.text: Confirm the signer personally appears and verify their identity
Confirm the signer is willing and appears aware of the document
Have the signer acknowledge that the signature is their voluntary act
Complete and seal the acknowledgment certificate and record the act in the journal

questions.explanation: The notary first confirms personal appearance and verifies identity, since nothing proceeds until the notary knows who is before them. Next the notary gauges that the signer is willing and reasonably aware of the act, because a coerced or confused signer must not be notarized. The signer then acknowledges that the signature is their free and voluntary act, which is the substance of an acknowledgment. Finally the notary completes and seals the certificate and records the act in the journal, documenting the completed notarization. This order reflects standard practice: identity and capacity come before the acknowledgment, and the certificate and journal entry memorialize what was done.

questions.stem: A signer asks the notary to come to a hospital room to perform a notarization at the signer's bedside. The notary is commissioned in that state and county. Is this generally permissible?

options.text: No, notarizations may only occur inside a bank or government office
Yes, a notary may perform acts at various locations within their jurisdiction, as long as all requirements (appearance, identity, willingness) are met
No, a notary may never travel to a signer
Yes, but only if the notary first diagnoses the signer's condition

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Notaries can perform acts at many locations within their jurisdiction, including hospitals, provided the usual requirements of appearance, identification, willingness, and awareness are satisfied. Why the others are wrong: **A** there is no rule limiting notarizations to banks or government offices; **C** notaries may travel to signers; **D** a notary is not qualified to diagnose medical conditions and that is not a requirement, though the notary must still judge apparent awareness.

questions.stem: Which two responsibilities reflect a notary's duty to safeguard the integrity of their office? (Select two.)

options.text: Keeping the official seal under the notary's exclusive control and never lending it
Promptly reporting a lost or stolen seal or journal as required by the state
Allowing a coworker to use the seal when the notary is on break
Leaving signed-and-sealed blank certificates ready for later use

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Maintaining exclusive control of the seal and reporting a lost or stolen seal or journal protect against misuse and uphold the integrity of the office. Why the others are wrong: **C** letting anyone else use the seal allows acts the notary did not perform and is prohibited; **D** pre-signed, pre-sealed blank certificates are a serious fraud risk and must never be created.

questions.stem: A notary performs three separate notarizations for the same signer during one visit (an acknowledgment and two jurats on different documents). How should this be recorded in the journal?

options.text: As a single combined entry, since it is the same signer and visit
As a separate journal entry for each individual notarial act performed
Only the first act needs an entry; the rest are implied
No entries are needed because the signer is the same person

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Each notarial act is recorded as its own entry, even for the same signer in one visit, so the journal reflects every act performed. Why the others are wrong: **A** combining distinct acts into one entry obscures the record and the different act types and documents; **C** every act, not just the first, must be logged; **D** a shared signer does not eliminate the need to record each separate act.

questions.stem: Why is a bound journal with sequentially numbered pages generally preferred over a loose-leaf binder for notarial records?

options.text: Because a bound, numbered book makes it difficult to insert or remove pages undetected, protecting the record's integrity
Because loose-leaf binders are illegal in every state
Because a bound book lets the notary charge a higher fee
Because loose pages cannot physically hold ink

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A permanently bound book with numbered pages resists tampering, since pages cannot be added or pulled without leaving evidence, which safeguards the chronological record. Why the others are wrong: **B** loose-leaf formats are not universally illegal, though a bound book is preferred for integrity; **C** the journal format is not a basis for higher fees; **D** loose pages can obviously hold ink, so that is not the reason.

questions.stem: A notary makes a mistake while writing a journal entry. What is the best practice for correcting it?

options.text: Erase or white out the error so the entry looks clean
Tear out the page and start over
Draw a single line through the error so it remains legible, then enter the correct information, preserving the original record
Scribble over the error heavily so it cannot be read

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Journal corrections should leave the original entry legible (a single line through the error) and add the correct information, keeping an honest, unbroken record. Why the others are wrong: **A** erasing or whiting out destroys the original and looks like tampering; **B** removing a page from a bound journal undermines its integrity; **D** obliterating the text hides what was originally written.

questions.stem: A notary's commission ends and is not renewed. What should the notary generally do with the completed journal?

options.text: Destroy it immediately, since the commission is over
Retain or deliver it according to the state's rules, keeping it available for the required retention period rather than destroying it
Give it to the next notary at the same workplace to reuse
Sell it to the public as a historical record

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Even after a commission ends, the journal must be retained (or delivered to a designated office) for the period the state requires, because it remains an important record. Why the others are wrong: **A** destroying records that must be retained is improper; **C** a journal is personal to the notary who created it and is not reused by another notary; **D** selling a record full of signers' private information violates their privacy.

questions.stem: When a notary provides a copy of a specific journal entry in response to a proper request, what is the best practice regarding OTHER entries on the same page?

options.text: Disclose the entire page, including unrelated signers' entries, for completeness
Provide only the requested entry and avoid revealing unrelated signers' personal information
Refuse the request entirely to protect privacy
Publish the whole page so the requester can verify nothing was hidden

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A notary should furnish only the specific entry requested and shield the personal information of unrelated signers recorded nearby. Why the others are wrong: **A** disclosing the full page exposes other signers' private data; **C** a flat refusal is wrong when the request is proper and lawful; **D** publishing the page is a gross privacy violation.

questions.stem: Which two practices best protect the security of a notary's journal? (Select two.)

options.text: Storing the journal in a locked, secure location under the notary's control
Keeping the journal in the notary's sole custody rather than leaving it with coworkers
Leaving the journal open at the public counter for convenience
Letting anyone photograph entries on request

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Locking the journal away and keeping it in the notary's sole custody prevent unauthorized access and protect signers' information. Why the others are wrong: **C** leaving it open at a public counter exposes private data and invites tampering; **D** allowing anyone to photograph entries breaches the confidentiality owed to signers.

questions.stem: A notary is asked to notarize a document for their own spouse, who is the signer and primary beneficiary. Why is this generally discouraged?

options.text: Because notarizing for a spouse or close relative with an interest can create a disqualifying conflict and the appearance of partiality
Because notaries may never notarize for anyone they have met before
Because spouses are legally incapable of signing documents
Because the fee must be tripled for family members

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Notarizing for a spouse or close relative who benefits raises a disqualifying interest and undermines the appearance of impartiality, so it should be avoided. Why the others are wrong: **B** notaries routinely serve people they know, such as long-time clients; **C** spouses are fully capable of signing documents; **D** family relationships do not change the permissible fee.

questions.stem: A signer hands the notary a document and points to a section asking, 'What does this clause mean for me legally?' The notary is not an attorney. What is the proper response?

options.text: Interpret the clause in plain language to be helpful
Explain that they cannot interpret the document's legal meaning and suggest the signer consult an attorney
Tell the signer the clause is standard and nothing to worry about
Rewrite the clause so it is easier to understand

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Explaining the legal meaning or effect of a document's clauses is the practice of law; a non-attorney notary must decline and refer the signer to an attorney. Why the others are wrong: **A** interpreting the clause is giving legal advice; **C** assuring the signer it is harmless is both legal advice and potentially false; **D** rewriting the document for the signer is unauthorized practice of law.

questions.stem: A signer arrives and admits, 'My brother already signed his own name on this; I'm just here to get it notarized for him since he couldn't come.' What should the notary do?

options.text: Notarize it, because the signature is genuine and the brother authorized it
Refuse, because the actual signer is not personally appearing, and notarizing another person's signature in their absence is improper and a fraud risk
Notarize it if the present person swears the brother signed it
Notarize it and note in the journal that the brother was absent

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The person whose signature is being notarized must personally appear; notarizing an absent person's signature, even a real one, is improper and a classic avenue for fraud. Why the others are wrong: **A** genuineness does not satisfy the appearance requirement; **C** a third party's sworn statement cannot substitute for the signer's appearance; **D** a journal note does not cure the absence of the actual signer.

questions.stem: A notary advertises a flat 'document package' price that bundles the notarization fee with vague 'processing services,' obscuring the actual per-act charge. Why is this problematic?

options.text: Because advertising notary services is prohibited
Because bundling can hide whether the notary is charging more than the allowed fee per act and misleads the public about the cost of notarization
Because notaries must always work without disclosing any price
Because flat pricing automatically makes the notarization invalid

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Bundling can conceal an overcharge above the permitted per-act fee and mislead the public about what the notarization actually costs, which conflicts with transparent fee practices. Why the others are wrong: **A** truthful advertising is allowed; **C** notaries can and should disclose their fees; **D** pricing structure does not by itself invalidate an otherwise proper notarial act, but the deceptive disclosure is the issue.

questions.stem: Which two requests should a notary refuse as improper or unlawful? (Select two.)

options.text: A request to notarize a signature the signer will make later, off-site, without appearing
A request to insert a false date so the document appears signed earlier
A request to notarize a routine affidavit for a properly identified, willing signer
A request to explain the difference between a jurat and an acknowledgment

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Notarizing a signature made without the signer appearing, and falsifying the date of the act, are both improper and fraudulent and must be refused. Why the others are wrong: **C** notarizing a routine affidavit for an identified, willing signer is exactly what a notary should do; **D** explaining the general difference between two acts is permissible and not legal advice.

questions.stem: Maintaining impartiality means a notary should serve the public without bias. Which action best reflects impartiality?

options.text: Refusing to notarize for people who hold political views the notary opposes
Notarizing for any qualified signer regardless of the notary's personal opinion of the document or the parties
Giving preferential service to friends and charging strangers more
Declining documents the notary personally disagrees with

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Impartiality means serving any qualified signer without letting personal views about the document or the parties affect the act. Why the others are wrong: **A** refusing based on the signer's politics is biased and improper; **C** favoring friends and overcharging strangers violates both impartiality and fee rules; **D** declining because the notary disagrees with the content injects personal opinion into a neutral duty.

questions.stem: A notary knowingly affixes their seal to a document for a person they know is impersonating the real signer. What category of liability does this knowing act most directly invite?

options.text: Only a minor administrative warning
Criminal liability, because knowingly participating in a fraudulent notarization can be a crime
No liability, since the impersonator is solely to blame
Liability limited to refunding the notarization fee

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Knowingly notarizing for an impersonator is intentional misconduct that can constitute a crime, exposing the notary to criminal penalties. Why the others are wrong: **A** a knowing fraud is far more serious than a minor warning; **C** the notary's knowing participation creates independent liability beyond the impersonator's; **D** consequences for criminal misconduct go well beyond refunding a small fee.

questions.stem: How do errors-and-omissions (E&O) insurance and a surety bond differ in whom they primarily protect?

options.text: Both primarily protect the notary against personal financial loss
A surety bond primarily protects the public, while E&O insurance primarily protects the notary from their own liability
Both primarily protect the public from harm
A surety bond protects the notary, while E&O insurance protects the signer's employer

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A surety bond exists to compensate members of the public harmed by the notary (who must repay the surety), whereas E&O insurance is optional coverage that protects the notary against their own liability. Why the others are wrong: **A** the bond protects the public, not the notary; **C** E&O protects the notary, not the public; **D** the roles are reversed and the employer is not the focus of E&O insurance.

questions.stem: A notary's surety bond has a stated coverage amount. A signer harmed by the notary's misconduct suffers losses exceeding that amount. What is the general result?

options.text: The harmed party can never recover more than the bond amount under any theory
The bond caps what the surety pays, but the notary can remain personally liable for damages beyond the bond amount
The notary is automatically relieved of all liability once the bond is exhausted
The signer's own losses are reduced to match the bond amount

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A surety bond limits the surety's payout, but it does not cap the notary's own liability; the injured party may pursue the notary personally for the excess. Why the others are wrong: **A** the bond is not the ceiling on total recovery from the notary; **C** exhausting the bond does not erase the notary's personal responsibility; **D** the victim's actual losses are not magically reduced to the bond figure.
